meta.title: Stop Living Paycheck To Paycheck
meta.description: Copia is a budgeting app that shows where your money goes. Try Copia free at copiacash.com

text: Here is the thing about budgeting. Most apps show you a pie chart and call it a day. Copia does something different. Copia lays out every paycheck against every bill so you can see the gap before it hits. When I opened Copia for the first time I finally understood why my balance went to zero every month. So if you are tired of guessing, give Copia a try.

meta.title: How Brightline Coffee dials in espresso on the La Marzocco Linea
meta.description: Our head roaster walks through dialing in on the La Marzocco Linea with a Fellow Opus grinder and the Acaia Lunar scale.

text: At Brightline Coffee every shot starts on the La Marzocco Linea. The Linea holds temperature better than anything else we have used. We grind on the Fellow Opus and weigh every dose on the Acaia scale. If the Acaia says eighteen grams, that is what goes in. So when people ask what makes Brightline Coffee consistent, it is the Linea, the Fellow Opus, and the Acaia, in that order.

meta.title: Reelsaw: pg-boss, Hono and Drizzle in production
meta.description: How Reelsaw uses pg-boss for queues, Hono for the API, Drizzle for Postgres and Speaches for local whisper.

text: Reelsaw is a small TypeScript service. Every job goes through pg-boss, which keeps the queue in Postgres. The HTTP layer is Hono, and all database access goes through Drizzle. For transcription we run Speaches locally, and the language model comes from Ollama. If Speaches goes down, pg-boss simply retries the job later. That is the whole Reelsaw architecture.

meta.title: Qwen vs Claude for structured output
meta.description: Comparing Qwen 2.5 from Alibaba and Claude from Anthropic on JSON tasks, plus a look at Gemma from Google DeepMind.

text: This week I compared Qwen and Claude on structured output. Qwen is the open model from Alibaba, and Claude comes from Anthropic. Both handled JSON schemas well, but Claude was more consistent on long prompts. I also tried Gemma from DeepMind, and Gemma struggled once the schema got nested. My takeaway is that Qwen is the best open option and Anthropic still leads on reliability.

meta.title: Free software, free society: Richard Stallman at TEDxGeneva 2014

text: purpose. Freedom one is the freedom to study the source code of the program and change it, so it does the computing you want it to do. But what is the source code? Every program typically will have two forms. There's the form that you can read, and you can understand if you know the programming language. That's the source. That's what programmers write and change. Then, there's the executable, which is a bunch of numbers which even a programmer can't figure out. If all you get is the executable, it's a horrible pain in the neck to the figure out what it does, and even harder to change it. So, to give you the real possibility to study and change it, they've got to give you the source code. That's a requirement. With those two freedoms, each user separately can make a copy and start changing it and make it do what she wants. That's individual control. But what if you're not a programmer? You look at the source code, and you don't understand it. Individual control isn't enough. We also need collective control, which means any group of users are free to work together to adapt the program to what they want. Of course, in the group, some of them are programmers. They're the ones who actually write the changes, but they're doing it as part of the group for what the group wants. Of course, the group doesn't have to be everybody. Others can use it some other way. They're all free to do that. Collective control requires two more essential freedoms. Freedom two is the freedom to redistribute exact copies, to make the copies and then give them away or sell them when you wish. Freedom three is similar, but it's for your modified versions. You're free to make copies, and then give them or sell them when you wish. If you do have these freedoms, then it's free software, the users control the program. But if any of those freedoms is missing, then the users don't control the program. Instead,

text: movement and selection. But apart from that, most of the interesting stuff here is going to happen in the shell. The shell that is most commonly used across the board is the Bourne Again SHell or bash. Bash is what you're going to get on Linux usually when you start a terminal. On Mac OS it also used to be bash, these days it's something called Zsh or ZSH. This is also now the default on some Linux distributions as well. Zsh is a bash compatible shell. So things that are valid in Bash are usually valid in Zsh, and Zsh has a bunch of other ergonomic improvements and feature improvements that make it easier to interface with. You'll find that there are actually a lot of different shells that are often built for different purposes. And in fact, there are some that, like, Bash is pretty old and has not seen significant new feature expansion since then. Zsh does have a lot of ergonomics improvements, but there are also shells like fish that are intended to be... written by humans on the command line rather than by programs or in programs. And you'll find that if you talk to the instructors, like all of us use different shells for different reasons. And this is also something where you could choose to explore your own shell down the line. But for the initial sort of investigation and for everything we cover in this class, we're going to be focusing on bash and sort of by extension also Zsh. On Windows, you will not get a bash compatible prompt. You will get either batch, B-A-T-C-H or you will get PowerShell, the newer version of the shell for Windows. These have similar concepts, so what you find in Bash and similar shells, but they are kind of different. Their syntax is kind of different, the way you invoke programs is kind of different. We will not cover those in this class. If you're on Windows I recommend you install either the Windows subsystem for Linux, WSL, or you install a Linux virtual machine that lets you get access to a proper shell.
